cards.title: Judge Ad Creative in Its Ecosystem, Not in Isolation
cards.summary: Winning paid creative often depends on the surrounding brand ecosystem, so don't assume a competitor's ads will work for a new or lesser-known brand.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to copy a competitor's paid creative or landing page approach, or diagnosing why your strong-looking ads underperform
steps: Recognize that a large brand's ads may perform mainly because of the ecosystem behind them—broad awareness, existing customers, repeat buyers, retail/franchise presence—not because the ad itself is strong. The source notes that if the same brand were relaunched tomorrow with the same assets, those ads would perform poorly in isolation.

Before copying a competitor's creative or lander, ask what ecosystem support you actually have: brand recognition, returning purchasers, email/SMS list, organic traffic, and existing first-party data.
If you lack that ecosystem, expect weaker cold-traffic response and compensate with tighter targeting, stronger offer specificity, or problem-first creative rather than brand-vibe creative.
Treat dramatic competitor results as contextual to their situation, not transferable benchmarks.
caveats: This is a presenter's opinion drawn from one brand teardown, not a universal law.
The 0.4% ROAS figure cited for a hypothetical relaunch is illustrative, not a measured benchmark.
cards.source_name: Alo Yoga Teardown_ Creative, Offers, Landers & Acquisition.docx

cards.title: Sending Paid Traffic to a Category Grid: When It Works
cards.summary: Driving paid traffic to a category grid is defensible for fashion brands with heavy on-site merchandising effort, but risky elsewhere—custom landers are the safer default.
cards.use_when: Choosing between a category grid and a custom landing page as the destination for paid ad traffic
steps: Assess whether you are in fashion or another fast-merchandised category where browsing a filtered grid matches buyer intent; the source considers this defensible only in that context and questionable otherwise.
If you are not in fashion, default to custom landing pages tailored to the ad's promise instead of a raw category grid.
If you do send traffic to a category grid, assign a specific team member to own its conversion rate and watch it closely.
Have that owner continuously adjust the filtering, sort order, and product ordering top-to-bottom as products go out of stock, size curves shift, and new products arrive.
Re-evaluate the grid regularly, because a stale grid with out-of-stock or poorly ordered items will erode click-to-cart conversion.
caveats: Fashion-specific advice; the source explicitly warns non-fashion brands to be careful.
Category grids require ongoing labor, so don't choose one unless you can staff the maintenance.

cards.title: Stop Rebuilding the Ad Account Every Few Weeks
cards.summary: The source advises against churning creative every ~24 days and rebuilding the account every ~3 weeks, arguing you should squeeze winning ads instead.
cards.use_when: Setting your paid-social creative refresh cadence and deciding whether to retire or retain winners
steps: Recognize that constant account rebuilds keep the account 'fresh' and align with a front-end brand-distribution strategy, but sacrifice the compounding performance of proven winners.
When you have a winning ad, keep running it rather than retiring it on a fixed schedule; the source says it has never seen double-downing on winners fail for a fashion brand.
If a winner is selling out, place quick replenishment orders to keep stock available—the source cites getting more inventory within about 3 to 4 weeks as the enabling condition.

When you find a winning product, keep ordering and running it for as long as the market wants it, since you have likely found a trend to lean into; use it to convert new customers who then become repeat buyers.
Reserve creative churn for fatiguing or losing ads, not for winners.
caveats: The 24-day creative cycle and 3-week account rebuild are descriptions of the teardown brand's practice, not recommended benchmarks.
Doubling down assumes reliable replenishment; without it you'll just run out of stock.
